text:
Vietnam plans to introduce a mandatory minimum share of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in civil aviation for the first time. The requirements are included in a draft environmental framework for the aviation sector that is currently under consultation.

For international flights departing from Vietnamese airports, the minimum SAF share would start at 1% in 2030, rise to 2% in 2031, 3% in 2032, 4% in 2033–2034, 5% in 2035–2037, 7% in 2038–2039 and 10% from 2040.

Domestic flights would follow a later schedule. The SAF share would be set at 1% in 2032–2034, 2% in 2035–2037, 3% in 2038–2039 and 5% from 2040.

The draft also provides for monitoring of SAF origin, volumes, quality and sustainability, as well as rules for trading, supply and blending. It also sets out a methodology for calculating emission reductions and a monitoring, reporting and verification system under CORSIA.

The proposed requirements are part of Vietnam’s broader policy to reduce aviation emissions and achieve Net Zero by 2050. However, the current draft does not include a separate incentive mechanism for airlines to use SAF ahead of the mandated dates or above the minimum levels.

title: Lighthouse Green Fuels project set to drive jobs and industrial growth across Teesside
description:
Lighthouse Green Fuels (LGF) has published new independent analysis revealing the economic impact its proposed multibillion-pound sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility could generate for Teesside and the wider UK.
The findings have been published on a new Impact section of the Lighthouse Green Fuels website, setting out how the investment could support jobs, skills, businesses and the long-term reindustrialisation of Teesside.
Developed by global manufacturing and infrastructure group Alfanar, Lighthouse Green Fuels will be located on a 270-acre brownfield site at Seal Sands.
It represents one of the largest proposed industrial investments in Teesside in a generation.
Lighthouse Green Fuels is exactly the sort of investment our region has fought hard to attract - creating skilled jobs, supporting local businesses and reinforcing Teesside’s reputation as the UK’s home of advanced manufacturing and clean industry.
text:
Lighthouse Green Fuels (LGF) has published new independent analysis revealing the economic impact its proposed multibillion-pound sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility could generate for Teesside and the wider UK.

Undertaken by Arup, the analysis forecasts that the project could generate more than £8 billion (€9.3 billion) in Gross Value Added (GVA) across the UK throughout construction and operations.

The findings have been published on a new Impact section of the Lighthouse Green Fuels website, setting out how the investment could support jobs, skills, businesses and the long-term reindustrialisation of Teesside.

Developed by global manufacturing and infrastructure group Alfanar, Lighthouse Green Fuels will be located on a 270-acre brownfield site at Seal Sands. It represents one of the largest proposed industrial investments in Teesside in a generation.

Once operational, the facility will convert around 1.5 million tonnes of sustainably sourced biomass each year into approximately 180 million litres of SAF and 30 million litres of renewable naphtha, helping establish new domestic fuel-manufacturing capability for the UK aviation industry.

The project is already at an advanced stage. Front End Engineering Design was completed in May 2026, confirming the engineering configuration and delivery strategy for the facility. Its Development Consent Order application has also been prepared as planning and permitting continue to progress.

In parallel, the project has submitted its application for connection into the Teesside carbon capture and storage network, while commercial discussions continue with major biomass suppliers and SAF offtake partners.

Ben Houchen, mayor of Tees Valley Combined Authority, said: "Teesside is showing exactly what can be achieved by backing the industries that will drive Britain’s economy in the years ahead. Lighthouse Green Fuels is exactly the sort of investment our region has fought hard to attract - creating skilled jobs, supporting local businesses and reinforcing Teesside’s reputation as the UK’s home of advanced manufacturing and clean industry.

The facility is expected to operate for more than 30 years, creating a long-term industrial asset at Seal Sands and supporting continued employment, investment and supply-chain opportunities across the region.

title: Canada Invests $4 Million in Next Hydrogen and CERT Systems Clean Fuels Projects
description:
Natural Resources Canada (NRC) announced it has awarded $4 million in funding to two projects in the Greater Toronto Area that will strengthen Canada’s clean fuels sector.
The projects, submitted by Next Hydrogen and CERT Systems, were accepted as part of the government’s Energy Innovation Program (EIP) Clean Fuels Call for Proposals.
CERT Systems’ project aims to advance a process that converts captured CO2 into ethylene.
Canada’s EIP advances clean energy technologies that will help the country maintain a competitive, reliable, and affordable energy system while transitioning to a low-carbon economy.
The Clean Fuels Call for Proposals funded projects spanning the clean fuels value chain, from fuel production to transportation and storage technologies, helping advance Canada’s position in the global clean fuels transition.
text:
Natural Resources Canada (NRC) announced it has awarded $4 million in funding to two projects in the Greater Toronto Area that will strengthen Canada’s clean fuels sector. The projects, submitted by Next Hydrogen and CERT Systems, were accepted as part of the government’s Energy Innovation Program (EIP) Clean Fuels Call for Proposals.

Next Hydrogen’s project is expected to develop a scalable fabrication process and improve the efficiency, performance, and cost of electrolyzer modules. According to a press release from NRC, by advancing low-carbon hydrogen production technologies, the initiative aims to support wider adoption of clean hydrogen energy, with emissions reductions of up to 95% compared with conventional hydrogen produced via unabated steam methane reforming when powered by low-carbon energy sources.

According to the company’s website, Next Hydrogen’s mission is to significantly reduce green hydrogen generation costs from renewable and other clean energy sources to enable widespread adoption of hydrogen solutions to decarbonize the global economy.

CERT Systems’ project aims to advance a process that converts captured CO2 into ethylene. The company reports that this process could result in an estimated 93.8% reduction in life- cycle emissions when compared with conventional jet fuel.

“Building Canada's energy future depends on building and scaling the technologies that will power our economy for decades to come. Investments in Canadian innovators like Next Hydrogen and CERT Systems are strengthening our energy security, supporting growth, and turning Canadian expertise into real-world solutions” said Canada’s Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson.

Canada’s EIP advances clean energy technologies that will help the country maintain a competitive, reliable, and affordable energy system while transitioning to a low-carbon economy. The Clean Fuels Call for Proposals funded projects spanning the clean fuels value chain, from fuel production to transportation and storage technologies, helping advance Canada’s position in the global clean fuels transition.

text:
🔥Explore how energy investors are navigating the markets at the Italy Investors Forum.

Italy’s Ludoil plans to invest €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion) in Sicilian oil refiner ISAB over the next five years after completing its acquisition of a 51% stake from Cypriot private equity firm GOI Energy.

The transaction returns control of ISAB to Italian ownership at a time of heightened energy market volatility and disruptions to refined fuel supplies from the Middle East. ISAB accounts for more than 20% of Italy’s refining capacity, making the refinery a strategically important part of the country’s energy infrastructure.

Ludoil said the investment will support the restart and modernization of several mothballed processing units, while also funding the production of sustainable aviation fuel and hydrogenated vegetable oil. The acquisition was cleared by the Italian government under its golden power regime.

The combination of ISAB and Ludoil will create an energy group with approximately €13 billion in annual turnover. Ludoil, founded in 1954, will take responsibility for managing ISAB’s three facilities in Sicily.

ISAB also has a long-term supply and offtake agreement with commodities trader Trafigura running through 2033. Under the arrangement, Trafigura supplies crude oil and other refining inputs while purchasing approximately 90% of ISAB’s refined petroleum products.

Under the agreement with GOI Energy, ISAB was valued at approximately €1 billion including debt. Financing for the acquisition was backed by a guarantee from Italian export credit agency SACE and provided by BPER, UniCredit and Monte dei Paschi.

text:
The start of 2026 brought the fourth anniversary of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, as well as new geopolitical tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, testing the resilience of the aviation industry, particularly in the global aviation fuel market[1]—six months since the start of the initial action, we look at some of the broader effects on the industry.

In June of this year, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) in an analysis of the first half of 2026 stated that fuel shocks may halve the profitability of the global aviation industry compared to 2025.[2] Fuel is the principal and largest operating cost of airlines, typically making up 20–40% of all outgoing expenses.[3] As the global economy reckons with the aftereffects of this year’s geopolitical instability, there may be decisions in the short and long term for the global aviation industry to mitigate any potential instability going forwards.

Jet Fuel in 2026

Entering 2026, the global aviation industry had enjoyed relative fuel price stability for much of the preceding 18 months, with prices staying between $80 and $95 per barrel,[4] a beneficial turnaround from the damaging price fluctuations following the end of the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Instability in the Strait of Hormuz led to the doubling of prices to over $180 per barrel[5] by April 2026—driven in part by fears that jet fuel shortages from failing supply chains could become a defining feature of the 2026 fuel market. A statement on 16 April 2026 from the International Energy Agency (IEA) that Europe had “maybe six weeks of jet fuel left,”[6] together with IATA’s warning that shortage-related cancellations in Europe could occur by the end of May,[7] triggered further price shocks and more increases.

Fortunately, concerns of increasing competition for dwindling stocks of jet fuel appeared to have been more sensational than rational, aided by governments in Europe and around the world looking to alternative means and adapting to the new reality. The coordinated decision by the IEA’s members to release over 400 million barrels of oil,[8] the largest such release in the organisation’s history, did not create a long-term replacement for the supply lost from the Middle East, but it allowed Europe, the US and Asia to adapt. European refiners increased jet fuel’s share of production, reaching record yields,[9] while American production hit and exceeded two million barrels per day for the first time,[10] resulting in record exports from the US to Europe and Asia. Even Middle Eastern producers such as Saudi Arabia diverted fuel exports to ports unaffected by the regional instability, with Saudi exports to Europe eclipsing pre-conflict levels by early June. These adjustments did carry higher costs, which are still evident today, with fuel prices remaining above $150 per barrel; however, the market did not experience the fuel shortages that many feared and some predicted.

Fuel Hedging

Many airlines have typically relied on fuel hedging to manage fuel-cost volatility, with European airlines having the highest hedging ratio globally. Before this spring, 70% of European airlines’ fuel needs for the year were hedged.[11] Fuel-hedging policies were adopted across both low-cost and legacy European carriers, meaning that significant amounts of their fuel consumption were covered by hedging contracts, and the evidence suggests European consumers avoided large-scale price increases in 2026 arising from supply constraints.[12]

North American carriers, unlike their European counterparts, have historically taken the opposite stance,[13] with the majority of North American (especially US-based) carriers having no hedging contracts in place.[14] Although North American airlines have posted strong profitability records in recent years,[15] their sensitivity to the dramatic rise in aviation fuel prices has impacted prices and profitability. Not only have US consumers faced a 25% increase in average ticket prices, reducing demand across the market, but multiple legacy operators suspended routes citing the increasing cost of aviation fuel as the direct reason for the suspensions.[16] Though not the only factor, the rise in fuel costs also was reported to have added to the pressures facing Spirit Airlines before it entered bankruptcy protection.[17] Whilst questions have been asked about the impact of the no-hedging strategy, there is little evidence that North American carriers will begin to follow their European partners or competitors into readopting large-scale fuel hedging.

SAFs

In addition to fuel hedging, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) was mooted as a strategic alternative for airlines mitigating fuel price shocks. The argument in favour of SAF being that, if the global oil and fuel market continues to maintain its instability, airlines may look towards alternatives like SAF, with its breadth of feedstocks and dispersed distribution potential, to lessen the impact of fossil fuel-based price shocks in the future.

This thesis misses the underlying fundamental issues that make SAF an unviable replacement in the short term. Even with the shocks to the aviation fuel market production, refining and supply capacities for SAF have remained consistently low. In 2025, 0.6% of the global jet fuel consumption consisted of SAF, according to the IATA,[18] which is expected to increase to 0.8% this year.[19] However, in recent months, airlines have shown renewed interest in SAF and have approached SAF producers with a view to securing more supply.[20]

SAF production, elements of which can be localised, also typically relies on high energy use for conversion of feedstocks into usable fuels and currently relies on global distribution networks to move stock from lower cost areas to areas of higher demand—both areas impacted by geopolitical instability.

Despite perception that higher, or at least unstable, jet fuel prices might spike demand for SAF, the significant delta between SAF prices and jet fuel prices remained, even if on a reduced basis—SAF prices have remained consistently high, with SAF averaging around $2,750 per metric ton or $375 per barrel,[21] which remains vastly higher than the approximately $150 per barrel found on the global aviation jet fuel market.

Widespread use of SAF in the aviation industry still requires large-scale investment to drastically increase the supply of SAF and, in turn, reduce the cost per barrel. But the sudden increases in the cost of jet fuel, and concerns about supply, will have caused the aviation market to notice that increasing investment in SAFs may provide a further offset to any future shocks.

Insurances

Some of the immediate impacts of the unrest in the Strait of Hormuz are discussed in detail in Ben El-Gamal’s discussion with Glen Brighton also in this newsletter.[22]

Increased war-risk insurance premiums have added a further strain on top of increased operating costs for airlines operating in the Middle East. Premiums have already risen between 50% and 500%[23] placing further restraints on operators based in or operating out of the Middle East.

In response, airlines have suspended or reduced routes to the Middle East where, for example, Dubai International Airport, a key transit-hub for European to East Asia routes, has seen a year-on-year fall of over 30%[24] in passenger traffic, falling outside of the top five busiest international airports in the world[25] after over a decade at the top.[26] Consolidation of some routes, and (a potentially temporary) exit by some carriers, will have softened some of the impact on profitability.

Lessor and Financier Perspective

Aircraft lessors face a different risk picture, being less immediately exposed. In the short term, the impact on lessors and financiers appears to have been limited, although aircraft lessors, including ACMI providers, may see an uptick in rent-relief, deferral requests or reduction in demand from airlines. Financiers may also need to consider requests for covenant waivers or amendments and, in more stressed cases, consensual restructurings where higher operating costs place sustained pressure on airline liquidity.

In other times, thoughts might have turned to whether there would be increased retirements of less fuel-efficient aircraft, in favour of aircraft that can better weather fuel-price shocks but heavy demand—including a reasonably quick return to flying by Middle Eastern carriers and still largely outpacing manufacturers’ supply capacity—has not seen wide-ranging retirements like those seen during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Other lessors see opportunities, potentially for economically beneficial sale-and-leaseback transactions of airline‑owned aircraft, for airlines seeking to replenish cash reserves or pursue further growth while prioritising cash and liquidity, which may have been depleted following profit declines this year.[27]

As a result, the primary focus of lessors and financiers is likely to continue to lie on the long-term consequences, rather than on the short-term impact, and on balancing growth opportunities while managing existing fleets.

Conclusion

In the short term, fuel price pressures, insurance costs and consumer appetite for Gulf-based (or routed) travel will remain key factors shaping airline and, to some extent, lessor and financier performance. Despite some anecdotal upticks in interest in production, SAF was always unlikely to provide a meaningful short-term response, but greater investment in a broader range of feedstocks and production locations may offer longer-term diversification from fossil fuel supply and price shocks. The question remains as to whether the geopolitical events that have raised the issues highlighted in the article are a one-off event or if these pressures are here for a while yet.

title: UK government releases preliminary data on 2026 SAF use | Biomass Magazine
description:

The data released Sept. 17 is the first provisional report released by the U.K. Department for Transport on 2026 SAF data.
Subsequent provision reports are planned for release periodically, with final data for 2026 scheduled to be released in November 2027.
The agency in July released its fifth provisional report on 2025 SAF data.
Full 2025 data is expected to be released by the U.K. Department for Transport in November.
text:
The U.K. Department for Transport on Sept. 17 released preliminary 2026 data regarding the country’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) mandate, reporting that 292 million liters (77.14 million gallons) SAF was supplied to the U.K. aviation market from Jan. 1 through Aug. 15.

SAF accounted for approximately 3.92% of total aviation fuel use during the period.

All the SAF supplied to the market from Jan. 1 through Aug. 15 was classified as regular SAF. No power-to-liquid SAF was supplied during the seven-and-a-half-month period.

The data released Sept. 17 is the first provisional report released by the U.K. Department for Transport on 2026 SAF data. Subsequent provision reports are planned for release periodically, with final data for 2026 scheduled to be released in November 2027.

The agency in July released its fifth provisional report on 2025 SAF data. That release indicates 333 million liters of SAF was supplied to the U.K. market last year, accounting for 2.26% of total aviation fuel use during the year. All 333 million liters were classified as regular SAF. Full 2025 data is expected to be released by the U.K. Department for Transport in November.

text:
On Thursday, Environment and Climate Change Canada announced that Ottawa is exploring rules to trade Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes, or ITMOs, the mechanism set out under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement that lets countries cooperate on their climate targets by trading verified emissions reductions and removals across borders.

Deep Sky, a Montreal-based carbon removal project developer behind an ambitious direct air capture facility in Innisfail, is celebrating the news.

“We’ve been working on this for over a year, getting Canada to move forward with a framework,” said the company’s government affairs specialist, Mathieu Bouchard.

The nearest-term opportunity for the firm is CORSIA, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation run by the International Civil Aviation Organization in Montreal.

The mandatory phase for that program kicks off in January 2027, requiring airlines flying certain international routes to use sustainable aviation fuel or offset emissions growth with carbon credits.

READ MORE: After carbon price rollback, Alberta carbon capture pitches clean fuel market as potential lifeline

CORSIA requires that a credit be only counted once, meaning Canada needs a framework before credits can be recognized under the scheme.

Bouchard says he doesn’t expect Ottawa’s framework would be finalized by January, but doesn’t see it as a major setback since credits can be accounted for retroactively.

“As long as there’s a framework in place within the next year, we should be fine,” he said. “But we need to keep pushing.”

Beyond CORSIA, he pointed to a growing web of bilateral carbon trading deals around the world.

Countries such as Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Peru, Ghana, Thailand, Morocco have signed on to such deals.

Bouchard says firms like his will be closely watching the trade negotiations between Canada and the EU, since the Bloc’s emissions trading system has recently announced it will open the door to carbon removal credits.

Domestic market still active, executive says

Asked whether the push into international markets reflects fading interest at home marked by a softer federal industrial price, Bouchard said no, pointing to growing interest from voluntary carbon credit buyers in the technology and finance sectors.

On the domestic regulatory side, Matthew said it’s still too early to gauge the impact of the industrial carbon-pricing agreement Ottawa reached with Alberta earlier this year, which set a slower price trajectory for the province’s Technology Innovation and Emissions Reduction (TIER) system than the federal government’s original benchmark.

He said the deal doesn’t change Deep Sky’s near-term business, but will matter over time as the company’s production costs fall and the regulated carbon price rises.

“The regulated carbon price needs to go up, and at some point we get into a world where it is cheaper for us to produce those credits and sell them to a buyer than it is to pay to purchase [in the system].”

text:
Pilatus has announced certification of a key component of its completely new cockpit for the PC-12 PRO, based on the Garmin G3000 PRIME Integrated Flight Deck, featuring capabilities such as Safety Autoland.

The Safety Autoland system has been certified by both the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

The PC-12 already ranks among the safest aircraft in class, with an exceptional, statistically proven safety record. With the PC-12 PRO, Pilatus takes this excellent safety standard to an even higher level: the latest generation of this bestseller is equipped with a host of additional safety features — including the innovative Safety Autoland system.

During final certification flights, Safety Autoland took centre stage as it underwent extensive testing. The goal was to demonstrate a fully automated landing in real-world conditions – from system activation all the way to a safe landing and automated communication and engine shutdown.

A smart system for emergencies

Safety Autoland is designed to handle situations involving sudden pilot incapacitation – due to a medical emergency, for example.

When the activation button is pressed or when a pilot inactivity is detected, the system takes full control of the aircraft, informing all occupants that the automated landing mode has been activated. Simultaneously, it begins analyzing all available information, including weather, aircraft status and navigation data.

Based on this information, the system determines the best choice of airport, taking into account factors such as runway length, wind, weather conditions and remaining fuel. It then calculates a safe route, avoiding obstacles and terrain.

During autonomous flight, Safety Autoland takes care of all the systems required for landing – including flaps, landing gear, lighting and de-icing – and fully prepares the aircraft for the final approach. It also handles all radio communications, automatically making calls on the appropriate frequencies to keep ATC and persons on the ground informed about the situation.

A proven engine on board

In a single-engine aircraft, a proven powerplant is the most important component. The PC-12 PRO is equipped with the latest version of the Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6 engine. With over 60,000 units in service and more than 400 million hours in the air, the PT6 engine family boasts an unmatched track record.

In addition, the PC-12 PRO produces fewer CO₂ emissions than comparable twin-engine turboprops and can operate on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF blends), enabling more sustainable flying with no loss of performance.

All these innovations ensure the brand-new PC-12 PRO is the most technologically advanced, best-performing and most reliable aircraft in its class. The PC-12 PRO has been reimagined, yet it is instantly recognizable.

title: Vietnam proposes first SAF blending mandate under new aviation environmental circular
description:

Alongside the SAF mandate, the draft set out a complete CORSIA monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) programme.

Singapore-based ASAFA is an independent non-profit organisation focused on promoting the adoption and integration of SAF across Asia.
text:
Vietnam’s Ministry of Construction – formerly the Ministry of Transport – was consulting on a draft circular that would consolidate the country’s environmental rules for civil aviation into a single framework, the 17 September report said.

The draft would address Vietnam’s commitment - as a member of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and party to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement - to reach Net Zero by 2050, and the challenge of managing aviation emissions, noise and green transition requirements across two separate regulations that had not kept pace with ICAO’s evolving Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) standards, AsiaSAF wrote.

At the time of the report, the legal basis for aviation environmental management in Vietnam rested on Circular 22/2020/TT-BGTVT, covering fuel consumption and CO₂ management, and Circular 52/2022/TT-BGTVT, covering wider environmental protection in civil aviation.

The new draft would combine both into a single, unified instrument, with clearer allocation of responsibility across the Civil Aviation Authority of Vietnam, airport authorities, aircraft operators, fuel suppliers, air navigation service providers and ground handlers.

While maintaining two separate Circulars as the scope of environmental regulation expanded risked fragmentation and inconsistent enforcement, a single framework would make compliance more manageable for industry as SAF, CORSIA and climate obligations became more detailed, the report said.

Under the version currently out for consultation, international flights departing Vietnamese airports would face a minimum SAF share starting at 1% in 2030, rising in stages: 2% in 2031, 3% in 2032, 4% from 2033-2034, 5% from 2035-2037, 7% from 2038-2039, and 10% from 2040.

Domestic flights would follow a separate, later-starting trajectory: 1% from 2032-2034, 2% from 2035-2037, 3% from 2038-2039, and 5% from 2040.

Although airlines would be encouraged to used SAF prior to the proposed dates or above the mandated minimum, no incentive mechanism was detailed in the current draft.

The draft also set out: SAF’s origin, volume, quality and sustainability monitoring; trading, supply and blending management and emission reduction calculation methodology.

Alongside the SAF mandate, the draft set out a complete CORSIA monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) programme.

The draft also extended monitoring to domestic aviation emissions, not just the international flights that fell under CORSIA’s scope.

As part of the proposal, airport operators would also gain a more defined role, taking on carbon accounting and climate risk.

Singapore-based ASAFA is an independent non-profit organisation focused on promoting the adoption and integration of SAF across Asia.

Furthermore, Bain Capital, EcoCeres’ main shareholder, is considering selling a portion of its stake during the operation. Deutsche Bank, HSBC, Morgan Stanley, and UBS are among the financial institutions working on the potential IPO.

EcoCeres takes its SAF business to the stock market

On the other hand, the initial public offering would test the interest of public markets in a company specializing in renewable fuels and with significant exposure to SAF this fuel serves as a lower-emission substitute for conventional jet fuel and can be used in existing aircraft without modifications. According to data collected by Reuters, SAF can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by around 80 % compared to conventional fuel.

The deal also comes as various markets move forward with requirements for incorporating SAFs into aviation, Singapore, Japan, and the European Union are among the jurisdictions that have established blending requirements to encourage their use. EcoCeres had previously considered a potential listing in London before turning its attention to Hong Kong.

Renewable fuel capacity reaches 770,000 tons

Likewise, the industrial scale of EcoCeres this constitutes another important part of its business profile, the company has a combined capacity of approximately 770,000 metric tons of renewable fuels annually between its facilities in Zhangjiagang, China, and Johor, Malaysia. title: Aviation sector: Higher jet fuel prices cloud airlines' recovery in 2026 - Credendo
description:
Passenger traffic benefited from strong demand growth in 2025. International travel led the recovery, with Asia-Pacific carriers posting the strongest regional growth.
As prospects for a diplomatic resolution of the Middle East conflict remain distant, jet fuel prices are expected to stay high in the short term, keeping pressure on airline profitability.
Leisure travel and visits to friends and relatives should remain key supports for demand growth over the medium to long term.
In Europe, ReFuelEU Aviation requires fuel suppliers to ensure that sustainable aviation fuel accounts for 2% of fuel supplied from 2025, rising to 6% in 2030, with an additional synthetic-fuel sub-mandate from 2030.
Despite today’s high conventional jet fuel prices, sustainable aviation fuel still costs around 1.5 to 2.5 times more.
text:
Airlines started 2026 with stronger demand and rebuilt financial buffers

The airline industry entered 2026 in its strongest position since the Covid pandemic, following a year of record passenger volumes, stronger profitability and rebuilt financial buffers. According to IATA, net profit rose by almost 40% in 2025, while the industry’s net margin improved from 3.4% to 4.2%.

Passenger traffic benefited from strong demand growth in 2025. International travel led the recovery, with Asia-Pacific carriers posting the strongest regional growth. Cargo also reached a record high in 2025, supported by e-commerce and shipments brought forward ahead of new trade tariff increases. However, those US import tariff hikes, the removal of de minimis exemptions and continued policy uncertainty later in the year weighed on trade flows, as reflected in stagnating US-Asia trade. Air cargo remains more cyclical than passenger aviation because of its exposure to global trade, e-commerce, high-value manufacturing, perishables and time-sensitive logistics.

Before the Middle East crisis began in March, the sector was already facing two structural challenges: decarbonisation and supply-chain constraints. Delivery delays for new aircraft and engines, limited maintenance capacity and cost pressures restricted airlines’ ability to fully meet demand. Aircraft deliveries fell to 1,254 in 2024, about 30% below pre-Covid peaks, while the backlog rose to a record 17,000 aircraft. IATA estimates that these disruptions added more than USD 11 billion in costs in 2025. Airlines responded by extending the lives of existing fleets and maximising load factors, but those measures remain temporary. Faster fleet renewal is still essential to expand capacity, improve operational efficiency and reduce emissions.

Hormuz disruption reshapes profitability

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz on 28 February 2026 abruptly changed the sector’s operating environment. The disruption removed a significant share of global jet fuel supply from the market, threatened fuel availability in Asia and Europe, pushed prices sharply higher, forced costly rerouting, disrupted Gulf airspace and tightened fleet capacity. The Middle East accounted for around 60% of Europe’s jet fuel supply in 2025.

A mid-June agreement between the USA and Iran briefly eased crude oil and petroleum product prices, including jet fuel. However, renewed attacks from July triggered a fresh price surge (see chart below). The pressure was further amplified by Russia’s ban on aviation fuel exports from 1 June to 30 November 2026, following Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and energy infrastructure.

For airlines, the crisis is primarily a margin compression shock. The industry operates with structurally thin margins, making weaker carriers more exposed to financial stress and a higher risk of failure. Low-cost carriers, airlines with limited hedging, Gulf-exposed operators and companies already dependent on refinancing or restructuring face the highest risk. Large diversified flag carriers and premium airlines are better placed to pass on part of the cost increase and absorb temporary disruption.

Airlines are passing part of the additional fuel cost on to consumers through higher fares. Passenger volumes remain high and continue to rise, although at a slower pace, with the Middle East as an exception. However, this will not be enough to maintain profitability at last year’s level. Regional performance is uneven. Middle Eastern airlines are expected to post a combined loss because of weaker demand and operational disruption, while all other regions should remain profitable, though below earlier forecasts.

Fuel prices dominate the short-term outlook

Ongoing disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, combined with Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and the group's seizure of parts of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, is maintaining pressure on global oil and petroleum product supplies and pushing jet fuel prices higher in the short term.

As prospects for a diplomatic resolution of the Middle East conflict remain distant, jet fuel prices are expected to stay high in the short term, keeping pressure on airline profitability. Hedged airlines will also feel the impact over time as existing contracts expire. Although services have gradually resumed across much of the Middle East, disruption continues on several routes. Dubai remains among the most affected destinations, with several European and Asian carriers extending suspensions into October and beyond.

Longer-term demand remains intact, but supply will cap growth

Sustained medium- to long-term demand growth remains the sector’s baseline scenario, provided geopolitical disruption gradually eases. Leisure travel and visits to friends and relatives should remain key supports for demand growth over the medium to long term. Cargo demand, which has also remained resilient despite slower growth in recent months, should gradually strengthen as well.

However, the sector’s pace of growth will increasingly be determined by service supply rather than demand. Demand may be strong, but constraints and bottlenecks in aircraft and engine deliveries, maintenance, repair and overhaul capacity will limit how quickly airlines can expand. Supply-chain disruption has become a new operating norm, and the mismatch between airline demand and aircraft manufacturers’ output is not expected to rebalance until well into the next decade. Positively, this constraint on capacity expansion reduces the risk of overcapacity.

Decarbonisation will add further pressure. Several regulations are pushing the sector in this direction. In Europe, ReFuelEU Aviation requires fuel suppliers to ensure that sustainable aviation fuel accounts for 2% of fuel supplied from 2025, rising to 6% in 2030, with an additional synthetic-fuel sub-mandate from 2030. This will raise compliance costs before these products are available at sufficient scale to materially reduce prices. Despite today’s high conventional jet fuel prices, sustainable aviation fuel still costs around 1.5 to 2.5 times more.

CORSIA, the global carbon-offsetting scheme for international aviation established by the International Civil Aviation Organization of the UN, is also entering a more demanding phase. Its first phase runs from 2024 to 2026, with 130 participating countries as of 1 January 2026. The scheme aims to reduce emissions to 85% of 2019 levels through 2035, implying the purchase of more carbon offsets as international air traffic, and therefore emissions, returns towards or above pre-pandemic levels. As a result, decarbonisation is not yet a margin-supportive transition lever. It is mainly a regulatory and fuel-procurement cost burden that further limits the sector’s already weak returns.

Beyond fuel and decarbonisation, medium-term profitability will remain fragile and closely tied to the global economy, especially in cargo. Airline prospects depend heavily on global economic conditions, with high inflation and elevated interest rates likely to dampen growth. Rising cross-border trade restrictions, particularly US import tariffs, also weigh on goods trade and cargo demand. Conversely, wider disruption at maritime chokepoints could support air transport as an alternative for some time-sensitive or high-value goods.

title: Technical Excellence at the Heart of Global Aviation: County Clare's Aerospace & MRO Powerhouse
description:
Built upon a foundational heritage that shaped modern commercial aviation, the region offers world-class airside infrastructure, purpose-built hangar capacity, and a complete lifecycle support network for global aircraft fleets.
His legacy continues to underpin County Clare’s distinctive aerospace proposition, where aviation, industry and regional development remain closely interconnected.
Human Capital & The Aviation Mechanics Apprenticeship Hub The true engine of County Clare’s aerospace cluster is its specialised labour force.
Facing a global shortage of licensed aircraft engineers, the Mid-West functions as Ireland's primary incubator for technical aviation talent.
As the sector accelerates digital transformation and operational sustainability, Shannon remains central to international aviation maintenance, asset management, and aerospace engineering.
text:
MRO Meetings Ireland: Why you should join the Irish and global aviation service community on February 23-25, 2027

County Clare, situated along the Wild Atlantic Way in the Mid-West of Ireland, has consolidated its position as one of Europe’s premier aviation and aerospace clusters. With Shannon Airport at its nucleus, the region anchors a globally integrated ecosystem spanning asset management, finance and leasing; advanced manufacturing, Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul (MRO), Continuing Airworthiness Management Organisation (CAMO) and emerging aerospace technology.

Built upon a foundational heritage that shaped modern commercial aviation, the region offers world-class airside infrastructure, purpose-built hangar capacity, and a complete lifecycle support network for global aircraft fleets.

Central to this foundational heritage was Dr Brendan O’Regan, whose pioneering vision positioned Shannon as an international model for airport-led regional development. Through initiatives such as the world’s first duty-free airport shop and the development of the Shannon Free Zone, O’Regan demonstrated how aviation infrastructure could be used as a catalyst for enterprise, employment, innovation and global connectivity. His legacy continues to underpin County Clare’s distinctive aerospace proposition, where aviation, industry and regional development remain closely interconnected.

The Birthplace of Aviation Finance and Regulatory Frameworks

This entrepreneurial platform created the conditions for Shannon’s later emergence as a global centre for aviation finance, led in the 1970s by Dr Tony Ryan and Guinness Peat Aviation. By pioneering the modern operating lease in Shannon, Dr Ryan did not just establish a commercial model, he created the global framework within which modern aviation finance operates today.

These crucial structural innovations paved the way for rapid growth, transforming aircraft leasing into the primary mechanism for international airline fleet financing. Key among these was leveraging Ireland’s extensive Double Taxation Treaty network, which today spans over 70 countries, to minimize cross-border tax frictions. Furthermore, Ireland’s early adoption and proactive implementation of ICAO Article 83 bis enabled the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) to transfer oversight responsibilities seamlessly when Irish-registered aircraft were dry-leased to foreign operators. This provided global financiers with structural security and legal certainty, establishing a blueprint that now sees over half of the world’s commercial leased fleet managed out of Ireland.

Importantly, Shannon’s legacy goes beyond paper finance, it mastered technical compliance. The region achieved a global benchmark when Shannon Aerospace became one of the first third-party MRO organisations in the world to be awarded the Joint Aviation Authorities (JAA) JAR-145 approval (the precursor to modern EASA Part-145 certification). This milestone set the global baseline for international airworthiness standards and cemented Shannon, Co Clare as an authority in heavy maintenance compliance.

Co-Location Synergy: MRO and Asset Management

A key strength of the Shannon cluster is its unique co-location model. Lessors and technical MRO operators share the same airfield tarmac. Lessors like AerCap and JP Lease Products & Services (JLPS) manage multi-billion-dollar portfolio assets within meters of heavy maintenance facilities including:

Atlantic Aviation Group (AAG)

Lufthansa Technik

Eirtech Aviation Services

International Aerospace Coating (IAC)

When an aircraft transitions between international operators, it can undergo deep structural base maintenance, C-checks, composite structural and component repairs, painting, and complete airworthiness management (CAMO) review without leaving the airfield. This one-stop-shop capability drastically reduces lease transition downtime, costs and ferry flight logistics.

In July 2026, Ryanair announced its intention to undertake a €50 million expansion of its engineering facility on a 6.7-acre airfield site at Shannon Airport.

Supported by Enterprise Ireland, the proposed project includes a 15,000 m² state-of-the-art 4-bay hangar, a dedicated engineering academy designed to train over 400 aircraft mechanics and create 80 new apprenticeship positions between 2027 and 2031.

Precision Manufacturing and Industry 4.0 Integration

Beyond the hangar floor, County Clare houses a network of precision engineering firms supporting Tier-1 aerospace interiors, airframe and engine OEMs.

Local precision machinists utilize multi-axis CNC machining, automated digital inspection systems, and advanced metallurgical processing to deliver high-tolerance engine and structural components. Adopting Industry 4.0 principles, such as real-time process monitoring, automated quality assurance, and end-to-end digital traceability, allows local suppliers to comply with stringent AS9100 quality management standards.

Advanced Materials, Predictive Maintenance, and Decarbonization

As global aerospace transitions toward lighter, more fuel-efficient architectures, engineering teams in Clare are leading specialized projects in composite structural repair, non-destructive testing (NDT), and component lifecycle management.

Digital Transformation: MROs across the cluster are integrating predictive maintenance platforms, IoT sensor analytics, and digital twin technology to transition from scheduled maintenance cycles to condition-based, real-time asset monitoring.

Sustainability & SAF: The region's technical infrastructure is aligning with European net-zero mandates, preparing for increased Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) blending, alternative propulsion support (hydrogen/electric architectures), and sustainable end-of-life aircraft recycling.

Human Capital & The Aviation Mechanics Apprenticeship Hub

The true engine of County Clare’s aerospace cluster is its specialised labour force. Facing a global shortage of licensed aircraft engineers, the Mid-West functions as Ireland's primary incubator for technical aviation talent.

With dedicated facilities driving the National Aircraft Mechanic Apprenticeship alongside the upcoming Ryanair Engineering Academy, the region continually develops Part-66 licensed A1 and B1/B2 mechanics and technicians. Partnerships between industry operators and regional higher education institutions ensure a steady supply of aeronautical engineers, technical asset managers, and composite repair specialists.

Positioning for the Next Phase of Global Aerospace

Combining historical precedence (GPA, JAR-145 approval), robust airside infrastructure (3.2 km runway with zero slot constraints), and continuous capital investment by the Shannon Airport Group, County Clare offers an unrivalled industrial base. As the sector accelerates digital transformation and operational sustainability, Shannon remains central to international aviation maintenance, asset management, and aerospace engineering.

This position will be further reinforced in February 2027 when the region hosts MRO Meetings Ireland 2027 at the University of Limerick. Bringing together global leaders in maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) and aviation services, the event will provide a valuable platform for networking, knowledge sharing, and business development. Combining industry insights with pre-arranged B2B meetings, MRO Meetings Ireland will create opportunities for companies across the aviation supply chain to connect, collaborate, and explore new business opportunities, further strengthening the Mid-West's reputation as one of Europe's leading aviation and aerospace hubs.

text:
FedEx is helping to power sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) procurement with the use of new agreements projected to secure more than 20 million gallons of neat SAF across five US airports throughout the calendar year of 2027.

This agreement will work across FedEx operations at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), Oakland International Airport (OAK), Miami International Airport (MIA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW).

The agreements are expected to deliver SAF at blend ratios ranging from 30% to 50%, depending on location.

FedEx is working towards its goal of sourcing 30% of jet fuel from blended alternative sources by 2030, while expanding the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) across its US air network.

"The latest agreements represent an expansion of SAF within the FedEx air network enabled, in part, by state and federal level incentives," says Greg Paulus, Vice President of Enterprise Sourcing.

Building on a strong year of SAF deployment

Since 2025, FedEx has secured approximately five million gallons of neat SAF through agreements that resulted in the deployment of 16.5 million gallons of blended SAF across five US airports. With this next phase of procurement, SAF blends now represent a significant share of FedEx's jet fuel use at the airports mentioned above.

"SAF is one of the most impactful decarbonisation solutions available to aviation today and an important part of our approach to reducing emissions," adds Karen Blanks Ellis, Chief Sustainability Officer and Vice President of Environmental Affairs at FedEx.

"For the market to grow, supply needs to be reliable, affordable, and sustainable. Expanding our procurement allows us to employ more SAF in our network while bolstering the demand for greater production and scale."

The new agreements are another step in putting more SAF into use across the FedEx network while demonstrating the demand that exists today. As the SAF market develops, FedEx will continue evaluating opportunities to expand its use where supply, infrastructure and economics align with the needs of its air network.

Coast-to-coast progress across five major airports

This continues the efforts of FedEx when it comes to harnessing SAF. FedEx introduced SAF at two US airports towards the end of 2025: Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

With these two additional deployments, FedEx began using blended SAF at a total of five major US airports in 2025. Combined, these agreements secure the equivalent of five million gallons of neat SAF.

"Expanding SAF use by FedEx to include our operations at DFW and JFK caps off a successful year of SAF deployments coast-to-coast," adds Karen.

"While we know there remains work ahead to procure more SAF and to continue to educate our stakeholders about how alternative fuels fit into our overall aviation sustainability strategy, we are proud of our steps forward in 2025."

Efficiency gains beyond the fuel tank

Along with increased procurement of alternative fuels to power its global fleet of more than 700 aircraft, FedEx has long pursued other efficiency improvement projects like aircraft modernisation and fuel savings initiatives. After achieving the goal of a 30% reduction in aircraft emissions intensity from a 2005 baseline in FY24, FedEx expanded the goal to a 40% reduction by 2034.

FedEx provides customers and businesses worldwide with a broad portfolio of transportation, e-commerce and business services.

With annual revenue of US$86bn, the company offers integrated business solutions utilising its flexible, efficient and intelligent global network.

Consistently ranked among the world's most admired and trusted employers, FedEx has more than 450,000 employees focused on safety, the highest ethical and professional standards and the needs of their customers and communities.

FedEx is committed to connecting people and possibilities around the world responsibly and resourcefully, with a goal to achieve carbon-neutral operations by 2040.

Partnering with FedEx

Hedera

FedEx joined the Hedera Governing Council, taking a seat alongside Google, IBM and Dell to help govern the enterprise blockchain network, with a focus on building trusted digital infrastructure for global supply chains.

OneRail

FedEx partnered with last-mile platform OneRail to launch FedEx SameDay Local, giving retailers two-hour and end-of-day delivery options via a network of 1,000+ drivers covering nearly 99% of the US.

Nimble

FedEx made a strategic investment in Nimble, an AI robotics and autonomous fulfilment company, to scale automation across its FedEx Fulfillment network of 130+ North American warehouse locations.

Amazon

Six years after ending their delivery relationship, FedEx and Amazon signed a new multi-year agreement covering residential delivery of select large packages, plus an expansion of free-returns options.

Aurora Innovation

FedEx has worked with Aurora Innovation on autonomous trucking, completing more than 3,200 driverless loads on Texas routes as part of its broader robotics-partnership strategy alongside Berkshire Grey, Dexterity and Nimble.

title: US Senate Advances Farm Bill 2.0 with Year-Round E15 in Focus
description:
Key Takeaways The Senate Agriculture Committee has advanced Farm Bill 2.0, formally titled the Agricultural Act of 2026.
Committee passage is an important step, but further Senate support will be needed before the legislation can become law.
What Is the Farm Bill 2.0?
The Farm Bill 2.0 would permanently authorize the year-round sale of E15 nationwide.
The proposal signals meaningful Senate committee support for year-round E15, biorefinery investment, SAF eligibility, and rural energy programs.
text:
The US Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry has advanced the Agricultural Act of 2026, moving the long-awaited Farm Bill 2.0 another step forward.

For the biofuels industry, one provision stands above the rest: permanent nationwide authorization for year-round sales of E15. Yet the bill's significance extends far beyond the ethanol blend wall.

Its energy title also seeks to strengthen federal support for biorefineries, clarify eligibility for sustainable aviation fuel financing, expand markets for biobased products, and simplify access to rural energy programs.

The proposal is not yet law, and its path through the full Senate remains uncertain. Nevertheless, its advancement provides a clearer view of how agricultural, energy, and rural development policies could intersect over the years to come.

Key Takeaways

The Senate Agriculture Committee has advanced Farm Bill 2.0, formally titled the Agricultural Act of 2026.

The bill would permanently authorize nationwide year-round E15 sales, addressing a persistent source of regulatory uncertainty for the ethanol market.

Title IX would clarify sustainable aviation fuel eligibility for the Biorefinery Assistance Program and restore support for pilot- and demonstration-scale biorefineries.

The proposal would also expand federal procurement of biobased products and streamline access to rural energy programs.

Committee passage is an important step, but further Senate support will be needed before the legislation can become law.

What Is the Farm Bill 2.0?

The Agricultural Act of 2026 is designed to update and extend federal agriculture and rural-development programs through fiscal year 2031. It covers the broad policy areas traditionally addressed through the farm bill, including:

Commodities

Conservation

Trade

Nutrition

Credit

Rural development

Research

Forestry

Energy

Crop insurance

The Senate Agriculture Committee describes the legislation as a response to economic conditions that have changed considerably since the previous farm bill became law in 2018. Its stated goals include strengthening the farm safety net, improving rural infrastructure, modernizing conservation programs, expanding agricultural research, and creating new markets for US-grown products.

For low-carbon fuel participants, the central question is:

How will the package in the Farm Bill 2.0 translate its broad goals into more durable demand and investment signals?

Why Does Permanent Year-Round E15 Matter?

The Farm Bill 2.0 would permanently authorize the year-round sale of E15 nationwide. E15 is gasoline blended with 15% ethanol, compared with the 10% blend commonly sold across the United States.

This provision matters because summer sales of E15 have repeatedly depended on temporary federal action. Seasonal uncertainty can complicate decisions for fuel retailers, distributors, ethanol producers, and agricultural suppliers.

Permanent authorization would establish a more predictable operating environment and remove the need to revisit the same regulatory question each year.

That does not mean E15 demand would increase automatically or uniformly. Retail infrastructure, consumer access, gasoline demand, regional economics, and implementation details would still influence market adoption. However, a permanent federal framework could give more businesses the confidence to plan around E15 as a lasting part of the US fuel mix.

For corn growers and ethanol producers, the provision also represents an opportunity to expand domestic demand for an established agricultural commodity and fuel pathway. Its broader market impact would depend on how quickly additional retailers and consumers adopt the higher-blend option.

How Would the Bill Support Bioenergy and Sustainable Aviation Fuel?

The bill's energy title reaches beyond conventional ethanol. According to the Senate committee's title-by-title summary, Title IX would improve the Biorefinery Assistance Program and explicitly clarify that SAF is eligible for program funding.

That clarification could be meaningful for developers facing the difficult transition from technical potential to commercial-scale production. SAF projects often require substantial capital, reliable feedstock strategies, and confidence in long-term demand. Federal financing support cannot resolve every development risk, but clearer eligibility can improve the policy framework surrounding investment.

The bill would also restore grants to develop, construct, or retrofit pilot- and demonstration-scale biorefineries. This addresses another important part of the commercialization challenge: helping technologies move from research and early testing toward larger-scale deployment.

Other energy provisions would strengthen the BioPreferred Program, which promotes the purchase and use of biobased products through federal procurement requirements and voluntary product certification. This will help to create markets for renewable agricultural materials while reducing reliance on petroleum.

Furthermore, the bill offers improvements to reporting on federal purchases of biobased products and simplifies applications under the Rural Energy for America Program. Together, these measures point toward a broader policy objective. Using federal procurement, financing, and technical assistance will create markets and reduce barriers for rural energy and biobased manufacturing.

What Should Biofuel Market Participants Watch Next?

It’s important to reiterate that committee passage is progress, not the finish line.

In his statement following the committee's action, Chairman John Boozman acknowledged that additional votes will be needed to move the legislation forward. The bill must still navigate the full Senate and any process needed to reconcile it with legislation from the House of Representatives before reaching the president.

Market participants should therefore distinguish between the direction of travel and enacted policy. The proposal signals meaningful Senate committee support for year-round E15, biorefinery investment, SAF eligibility, and rural energy programs. The timing, final language, funding, and implementation of those provisions remain subject to the legislative process.

The most immediate issues to monitor include:

Whether year-round E15 remains intact as the bill advances

How the Senate builds the broader support needed for passage

Whether the SAF and biorefinery provisions change during negotiations

How final funding and implementation details affect access to federal programs

How the final legislation aligns with wider US biofuel, agricultural, and tax policy

The Farm Bill 2.0 is broad by design. But its biofuels provisions are more than secondary additions.

They connect agricultural demand, rural investment, fuel policy, and emerging low-carbon technologies. If enacted in their current form, they could provide greater certainty for existing ethanol markets while helping the next generation of bioenergy projects move closer to commercial deployment.

Follow the Policies Reshaping Biofuels Markets

Policy developments rarely affect one part of the biofuels value chain in isolation. Changes to blending rules, agricultural markets, project financing, and low-carbon fuel support can influence demand, feedstock competition, investment, and trade.

title: Engineers just mapped a narrow path to greener flying - Anthropocene Magazine
authors: Anthropocene Team, Sarah DeWeerdt, Douglas Fox
description:
The researchers estimated the effects of sustainable aviation fuels and modern efficient engines on aircraft pollution.
These emissions impact human health on the ground.
Both planes flew on lean-burn engines, but one used conventional fuel while the other used sustainable aviation fuel.
Their new analysis shows that the advanced engines reduce soot particle emissions by three orders of magnitude compared with conventional engines.
By comparing particle emissions from different aviation fuels and aircraft engines, the findings enhance the understanding of aircraft emissions in the low-soot regime.
text:
Flying is one of the fastest-growing sources of greenhouse gas emissions, according to the European Commission. And while road transport emits more carbon over, flying is energy-intensive per person. Flying from Lisbon to New York and back produces roughly the same emissions as an average European Union citizen heating their home for a year.

The aviation industry has adopted several measures to cut its emissions. But data on the impact of these measures has been limited.

Researchers from the German Aerospace Center provide some new insights in a study in the journal Science Advances. The researchers estimated the effects of sustainable aviation fuels and modern efficient engines on aircraft pollution.

“Our findings demonstrate that a substantial reduction of particle emissions requires a synergistic approach, combining the use of alternative fuels with modern engine technologies,” the team writes. “The results may support the optimization of future engine technologies for lower particle emissions…and thereby help to reduce the impact of aviation on climate and public health.”

In addition to carbon dioxide, jet engines emit ultrafine particle pollution, composed mainly of tiny soot and sulfate particles. These emissions impact human health on the ground. Under the right atmospheric conditions, the particles also lead to contrails. That’s because hot water vapor in engine exhaust condenses on the tiny solid particles and freezes. Contrails can persist for hours and trap heat in the atmosphere.

Reducing aviation’s non-carbon dioxide emissions will be key to meet the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C, past studies have shown. Sustainable aviation fuels and modern lean-burn engines, which use a higher air-to-fuel ratio, should both reduce particulate emissions.

But “the influence of the fuel composition…on particle emissions in rich-burn and lean-burn combustor conditions has hardly been explored in flight experiments,” Rebecca Dischl and colleagues write in the paper.

So the team analyzed measurements of in-flight particulate emissions from two Airbus airplanes. Both planes flew on lean-burn engines, but one used conventional fuel while the other used sustainable aviation fuel.

As the airplanes cruised, a smaller test aircraft equipped with inlets on the fuselage followed. The test craft had various instruments for measuring aerosol particles and trace gases. Two instruments mounted under the wings detected ice particle number and size. The test flights were conducted in November 2021 and March 2023.

Earlier this year, the research team reported that aircraft made contrails even when they produced less soot. Liquid particles such as engine oil droplets, it turns out, led to contrail formation.

Their new analysis shows that the advanced engines reduce soot particle emissions by three orders of magnitude compared with conventional engines. Further, under the rich-burn conditions, soot particle emissions depended exponentially on the hydrogen content of the fuel burned.

Meanwhile, volatile particle emissions from sustainable fuels increased with the sulfur content of the fuel. And the emissions varied considerably even between engines of the same type, the authors found.

By comparing particle emissions from different aviation fuels and aircraft engines, the findings enhance the understanding of aircraft emissions in the low-soot regime. This data should serve as valuable input for advancing jet engine model development, the researchers write. Optimizing fuel composition and engine technology would reduce particle emissions, improve airport air quality, and mitigate contrails.

Source: Rebecca Dischl et al. Mitigating aviation’s environmental impact through alternative fuels and cleaner engines. Science Advances, 2026.

text:
To help energy communities overcome establishment hurdles and trade power directly, technology innovator Grid Singularity is developing energy exchange marketplaces and championing blockchain-based digital solutions.

This work is vital because peer-to-peer energy trading and energy communities are a fundamental part of the new decentralised energy system. However, despite their authorisation in EU legislation – with variable uptake and promotion in member states – true energy communities that feature member trading and participate in broader flexibility markets remain few and far between, not least because of the complexities involved in their establishment.

“Energy communities in Europe are growing in number but unfortunately not in size due to administrative and legal complications,” says Grid Singularity co-founder and CEO Ana Trbovich.

She also notes there is very little true peer-to-peer trading between individual household assets in Europe and the majority of P2P is rather peer-to-pool, meaning that trade happens against a single price for the entire community.

One of the barriers is that the companies that manage the assets on behalf of the communities tend to silo them, effectively limiting the services it can offer rather than sourcing more sophisticated solutions in demand response and energy trading.

The asset management companies also tend to choose a simplified approach that they can operate directly for their own profit - which is rational market behaviour, but not in the best interest of the community members.

In this case, the prosumers never profit but only save, she says: “They have better pricing, but they are always paying something as opposed to actually making money on the market, which would be possible if a more sophisticated tool is applied.”

Importantly, she says, trading between communities – “which would really unleash the potential of these communities to be a solution provider rather than a pressure point for grid management” – is not currently permitted in EU member states, despite permissiveness of relevant EU directives.

Advancing energy communities

So how can these be overcome?

One simple option is for the companies managing the assets to serve as a conduit for additional, third-party services to the community members.

“I wish we would see more private and business initiatives such as university campuses or business parks taking the opportunity to monetise their energy assets by becoming a local energy market,” says Trbovich.

“Also, it's important to note that while there are more and more PVs, the battery capacity is still low and there is very little in terms of shared batteries, which would really make this model more lucrative by significantly reducing the term of the battery ROI.”

Currently, prosumers in many parts of Europe can benefit from low PV prices or free electricity, but only during limited hours - a constraint that battery storage could help mitigate.

When it comes to setting up an energy community, Trbovich says the conditions and level of support vary with the jurisdiction and how the EU directive has been implemented. As knowledge is generally limited at the public level, most are set up by a company managing assets as an additional revenue source or to gain a competitive edge, or by a knowledgeable and enthusiastic community member.

Ultimately it has to be made easier, she says. For example, there may be restrictions to add PV to older buildings and there are the restrictions on shared community batteries. Most building associations do not venture into that direction because it appears too complex. Balcony PV regulation is an example of how it can be simplified for citizens to take action.

Then there is the need for the smart metering and other hardware, including IoT interconnectivity – in Switzerland for example, she points out, there are PVs without connectivity that could not be integrated in an energy community – and arguably most importantly to open up energy community flexibility, a flexibility register at either or both the EU and country levels.

Data integration

This registry would identify and connect all distributed energy assets on a secure platform, to which companies like Grid Singularity could connect to and offer a service. Currently, to offer a service to a community the data integration would be needed with that community but because the communities are such small scale, the effort would often not justify the cost of the service, Trbovich says.

“Facilitating data integration is critical, not just for our service but for any service offering more sophisticated energy trading mechanisms or demand response services that can help customers engage in both behavioural change and other types of asset optimisation to make the best out of the resources that they have – and be encouraged to invest in more.”

She adds being understanding of the slow pace of regulators because of the need to take account of supply security, but at the same time, says it is frustrating that there are no goalposts or milestones for the progressive reform that is required to scale more advanced energy trading and demand response services for citizens.

For that, primarily member states need to be more permissive, and while the EU level regulation is sufficiently broad, she feels the Commission could also do some simplification.

“I do not see a need for separate definitions for citizen energy communities versus renewable energy communities versus self-consumption schemes and that language ends up complicating and adding barriers to entry for citizens. The Commission and member states should just say how you as a citizen can participate in a local spot market or flexibility market without separating these into different boxes that end up creating administrative hurdles.”

Blockchain in the energy sector

Turning to the broader implementation of blockchain in the energy sector, Trbovich, a co-founder a decade ago of Energy Web which has been at the forefront, says that while there are sectors such as finance where it is still controversial, in the energy sector it has been relatively straightforward.

“The blockchain use cases are about transparency and automation and solving complex problems in a more secure way, ensuring that your data is not in silos where there is a central point of failure, but can stay distributed.

“You can connect assets, give them a decentralised ID and ensure that access rights are effectively managed by assigning roles and levels of access to the selected information, and this is something that blockchain can do much better than any other programming tool that we have,” she says.

As an example, she mentions a real case implementation with the Australian energy market operator (AEMO) over a number of years which has enabled flexibility coordination of the fast growing number of distributed energy resources and offers it as a good example for European or other global operators to follow.

Another example, currently being implemented, is the Energy Web Verified Compute Cloud running in conjunction with the sustainable aviation fuel registry for management of the sustainable aviation fuel supply chain and transparent ESG reporting.

However, Trbovich points out there also have been cases of blockchain misuse by some companies, particularly for marketing greenwashing, such as taking a process that occurs unmonitored off-chain and putting only the end result on the blockchain with a timestamp to falsely claim that the process was implemented credibly by generating an unbacked certificate.

“That is a poor, unethical use of the technology,” she comments, adding that ultimately blockchain is a backend component of a service that operates in multiple energy and other services offered without users being aware.

She also emphasises that its potential is still not fully utilised, with one of the main reasons being the strong vendor lock-in in many applications that prefer siloed data and processes.

AI in energy

The other big topic in the energy sector is AI and Trbovich says that when it arises it is mainly around automation and machine learning in modelling.

“AI a tool that is enhancing diverse energy services and works hand in hand with blockchain. For example, Grid Singularity works with forecasting services and therefore integrates AI indirectly rather than directly, since these services benefit from machine learning. Like other companies we also use it for research and simple design and programming tasks but with heightened quality control by our team.”

Considering the broader digitalisation challenges in energy domain, Trbovich says there is a need for more interoperability, prioritising setting up of the decentralised DER flexibility registry, ideally at EU level. She also underscores the need for simplified battery sharing options for further local market optimisation.

“We will always need the grid but we will need less investment in physical infrastructure if we can manage it better, especially at the local level.”

text:
OMV Petrom SA said it had laid the foundations and installed the main processing equipment for a project to enable biofuel production at Romania's Petrobrazi refinery, keeping it on track for commissioning in 2028.

"With a EUR 560 million [over $635 million] investment, we are building a new unit that will produce 250,000 tonnes per year of sustainable fuels made from renewable feedstocks", OMV Petrom executive board member Radu Căprău said in a press release. "These lower carbon fuels will contribute to reducing emissions in sectors where electrification is difficult, such as aviation and heavy transport.

"We have completed the foundations, for which approximately 20,000 cubic meters of concrete were poured, and equipment up to 60 meters high is already installed in the refinery".

The new unit will produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) using vegetable fats and used cooking oils as feedstock.

"The flexibility of the new unit will allow the adjustment of the feedstocks and of the final product mix, from SAF and HVO to bio-naphtha and bio-LPG, depending on market requirements and feedstock availability", OMV Petrom said.

"The use of these fuels allows for a significant reduction in CO₂ emissions compared to traditional fossil fuels (by at least 65 percent).

"Construction works started in 2025. In the coming period, works will continue with the installation of equipment, the connection of the new units to the refinery’s existing infrastructure, as well as an extensive testing and verification program before commissioning, estimated for 2028".

Concurrently OMV Petrom is enabling hydrogen production at the site in Brazi, Prahova, with the modules for two electrolyzers installed this year. OMV Petrom expects to invest EUR 190 million in the hydrogen projects.

Accounting for about 35 percent of Romania's fuel demand, Petrobrazi has an annual capacity of 4.5 million metric tons, according to OMV Petrom.

OMV Petrom aims to reach a production capacity of 300,000 metric tons per annum (tpa) of biofuels and around 15,000 tpa of renewable hydrogen by 2030.

OMV Petrom is majority-owned (51.2 percent) by Austria's state-backed OMV AG, while the Romanian government holds 20.7 percent.

OMV has already been producing SAF since 2022 through its Schwechat refinery in Austria. The facility co-processes locally sourced raw materials such as used cooking oil.

OMV supplies SAF to several airlines in Austria and has secured agreements to deliver a cumulative 1.5 million metric tons by 2030, according to the company.

Under the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation adopted October 2023, aviation fuel suppliers at larger European Union airports must have at least two percent SAF in their total mix starting 2025. That must increase to six percent from 2030 and 70 percent from 2050.
